One approved workload model, four load tools. Every renderer reads the same §4 model as its only contract and emits synthetic=true baggage on every request so the generated traffic stays identifiable. Each one also publishes a capability report that declares, honestly, where it approximates the model instead of matching it exactly. Exporter Fit Arrival model synthetic=true k6 native open & closed, native OTel baggage + span per request JMeter established teams open via Concurrency TG + Throughput Shaping Timer; closed native baggage request header Gatling Scala sims open & closed, native protocol header + trace-context Locust Python shapes open approximated via LoadTestShape + pacing; closed native OTel baggage per request A note on honesty Every renderer ships a supports() capability report that names its approximations before it renders. A closed-native tool asked to reproduce an open arrival model will say so. We'd rather you see the seam than trust a perfect-looking fit that isn't.

Renders the model to an Apache JMeter .jmx test plan plus CSV data sets, with a manifest recording provenance and the capability report. An open arrival profile maps to a Concurrency Thread Group driven by a Throughput Shaping Timer; a closed model maps to native concurrent users. Payload pools become CSV Data Sets. synthetic=true is carried as a request baggage header. Arrival model open via Concurrency Thread Group + Throughput Shaping Timer; closed native Feeders / payloads one CSV Data Set per payload pool synthetic=true baggage request header See skills/jmeter-synthesis and How it works for where this sits in the loop.

documents.t: k6 is the default renderer. It emits versioned, reviewable k6 scripts plus synthetic payload pools: ramping-executor arrival profiles, request chaining with fail-fast correlation, and cache-avoidance payload pools (Zipf-distributed keys with cache-hit-ratio targeting). Open and closed arrival models both map natively. synthetic=true rides as OTel baggage and span emission on every request. The V2a static gate runs node --check (or mcp-k6 validate_script when available). Arrival model open and closed, native Feeders / payloads pre-generated Zipf pools with cache-hit-ratio targeting synthetic=true OTel baggage + span emission per request See skills/k6-synthesis and How it works for where this sits in the loop.

Renders a locustfile.py with one HttpUser and a weighted @task per journey, plus lib helpers and the same pre-generated feeders the k6 renderer emits. Open arrival is approximated with a LoadTestShape plus constant_pacing (declared as approximation G-O1); per-stage user counts come from Little's Law, clamped to the VU cap. Correlation uses fail-fast require_value extraction. synthetic=true rides as OTel baggage on every request. Arrival model open approximated via LoadTestShape + pacing; closed native Feeders / payloads the same pre-generated Zipf pools as k6 synthetic=true OTel baggage per request (best-effort OTel emission) Declared approximations open-arrival shaping (G-O1); empirical think-time sampling (G-E1) See skills/locust-synthesis and How it works for where this sits in the loop.

First get the tool, then walk the loop. Start with the no-backend example to see what each stage produces, then run the full live loop against your own tenant when you're ready. For what you need before the live loop — tokens, scopes, and agent tooling — see Requirements. To install the skills into your coding agent, see Installing the skills. For every engine install path (per-platform binary, Docker, Kubernetes, source), see The engine.

Pick the path that fits. The fastest way to run SCOPE is the released engine — a standalone binary or a container, no Python toolchain required. To drive the whole loop from your coding agent, install the skills. To hack on the code, clone the source.

The engine ships as a standalone workload-engine binary and a multi-arch container (amd64 + arm64) on every release. The current pinned tag is v0.1.0; use latest to always track the newest. Docker: docker pull ghcr.io/henrikrexed/ai-performance-testing:v0.1.0 # or :latest Binary — download the one for your platform from the latest release. Each binary ships a CycloneDX SBOM (<binary>.cyclonedx.json) next to it: VERSION=v0.1.0 curl -fsSL -o workload-engine \ "https://github.com/henrikrexed/AI-Performance-Testing/releases/download/${VERSION}/workload-engine-linux-amd64" chmod +x workload-engine && ./workload-engine --help macOS (Apple Silicon), Windows, and a one-shot Kubernetes Job are all in The engine §1.

documents.t: One command fetches the repo and installs the skills into your agent (default ~/.claude/skills), verifying each one: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/henrikrexed/AI-Performance-Testing/main/install.sh | sh It prints the exact next command — the first prompt of the guided loop. Per-agent paths (opencode, Cursor, cross-client) are in Installing the skills.
documents.s: Install the skills into your coding agent

documents.t: git clone https://github.com/henrikrexed/AI-Performance-Testing.git cd AI-Performance-Testing You'll need Python 3.11+, Node.js 20+, and (only for the EXECUTE stage) k6. Without k6 the skills degrade gracefully to a node --check syntax pass. This is the checkout the no-backend example below uses.

Run the first half of the loop on the bundled synthetic example — no tenant, no tokens. From a source checkout: # SCOPE: synthetic extraction -> a G0-validated model + a human-readable proposal (cd skills/workload-model && python3 scripts/build_example.py \ && cat out/example-frontend/scenario-proposal.md) # SYNTHESIZE: turn the committed example model into a runnable k6 script (V2a gate) (cd skills/k6-synthesis \ && node bin/synthesize.mjs ../../examples/workload-model.example.json /tmp/example-out) Read the proposal, then look at what SYNTHESIZE generated. The example artifacts under examples/ show exactly what each stage produces. This is also where you'll see the V1 gate in action: synthesis refuses a model that hasn't been approved.
documents.s: Try it with no backend (~10 minutes)

documents.t: When you want the real thing, point KnightLoad at your own backend: Copy .env.example to .env and fill in DT_ENDPOINT and DT_API_TOKEN (plus an OTLP token if you're exporting). A Dynatrace trial works. See Requirements. Install the skills into your coding agent (Claude Code, opencode, Cursor, or any agentskills.io agent). See Installing the skills. Ask for the loop in plain language — "scope a load test for service checkout over the last 3 hours" — and walk the five stages: SCOPE → VALIDATE → SYNTHESIZE → EXECUTE → ANALYZE. The full worked tutorial deploys a small demo AI-agent app, generates a baseline window, and runs all five stages for real — including the V1 approval gate refusing synthesis until you sign off. Before you share anything Run bash tools/secret-scan.sh from the repo root and make sure it exits clean. Next: Read the methodology · Full tutorial · Token scopes & requirements

documents.t: The engine and the renderer skills are deliberately dependency-light (see engine.md and skills-install.md). This page covers the backend access and agent tooling they sit on top of. New here? Start with the two-command quickstart in skills-install.md — it installs the skills and runs the whole loop on a bundled synthetic example with no tokens. You only need the backend access below once you point the loop at your own tenant. A .env.example at the repo root lists every variable; copy it to .env and fill it in. Never commit a real .env.

The reference observability backend is Dynatrace Grail (DQL). You need up to two separate tokens — a read-only token for extraction/analysis, and (only if you ship the generated load's telemetry back) an OTLP ingest token.

A platform token used for SCOPE extraction and the ANALYZE shape-diff. Minimum scopes: Scope Needed for storage:spans:read journeys, archetype split, baselines — required storage:logs:read access-log entrypoint cross-check — recommended storage:user.sessions:read RUM session shape (skills/rum-sessions) storage:user.events:read RUM ordered user actions / journey stitching (skills/session-stitch) — add this if you want RUM-driven journeys storage:user.events:read is the one that is easy to miss: without it the RUM user-action stream returns 403 and session stitching falls back to spans only. The full per-safety-level scope matrix lives in the dtctl Token Scopes doc. Set it in .env as DT_ENDPOINT + DT_API_TOKEN.

Only needed if you send the generated load's telemetry (it carries baggage: synthetic=true) back to your environment for the ANALYZE step. This is a different token from the DQL one above. Scope: ingestion:otlp:write Endpoint: https://<env>.live.dynatrace.com/api/v2/otlp Set as DT_OTLP_ENDPOINT + DT_OTLP_API_TOKEN.

If you let dtctl use Dynatrace's built-in intelligence (Davis Analyzers / Davis CoPilot — e.g. natural-language → DQL), the read token also needs the Davis scopes, e.g. davis:analyzers:read, davis:analyzers:execute, and davis-copilot:conversations:execute (plus davis-copilot:nl2dql:execute for NL→DQL). See Dynatrace intelligence, below.

dtctl is the open-source Dynatrace platform CLI (dynatrace-oss/dtctl). It is how the workload-model skill runs the DQL extraction that produces the engine's input. Install: # Homebrew (macOS / Linux) brew install dynatrace-oss/tap/dtctl # or a binary from the releases page: # https://github.com/dynatrace-oss/dtctl/releases/latest # or from source: git clone https://github.com/dynatrace-oss/dtctl.git && cd dtctl && make install Authenticate & set a context: # OAuth (recommended — browser SSO, no token to manage) dtctl auth login --context my-env --environment "https://abc12345.apps.dynatrace.com" # or token-based (use the read-only DQL token from §1) dtctl config set-context my-env --environment "https://abc12345.apps.dynatrace.com" --token-ref my-token dtctl config set-credentials my-token --token "YOUR_READONLY_DQL_TOKEN" dtctl doctor # verify configuration / connectivity / auth dtctl query "fetch spans | limit 1"

dtctl ships its own Agent Skill (skills/dtctl/, agentskills.io standard) that teaches a coding agent how to drive it. Install it with the CLI — it auto-detects your agent, or you can target one: dtctl skills install # auto-detect the current agent dtctl skills install --for claude # Claude Code dtctl skills install --for cursor # Cursor dtctl skills install --cross-client # shared .agents/skills/ (any compatible agent) dtctl skills install --global # user-wide instead of project-local dtctl skills status # check what's installed dtctl skills install --list # list supported agents This is separate from installing this repo's skills/* (workload-model, k6/jmeter/locust/gatling-synthesis, loadtest-run, baseline-diff, rum-sessions, session-stitch) — see skills-install.md for those.

Beyond raw DQL, dtctl exposes Dynatrace's Davis AI — Analyzers (predictive analytics) and Davis CoPilot (generative assistance, including natural-language → DQL). These are useful when a coding agent is drafting extraction queries. Access from the CLI via dtctl exec copilot nl2dql "error logs from last hour" and the related exec/analyzer commands. They require the Davis scopes on your token (see §1): davis:analyzers:read, davis:analyzers:execute, davis-copilot:conversations:execute, and the specific CoPilot sub-scopes (davis-copilot:nl2dql:execute, etc.). The dtctl Agent Skill (above) already documents these commands, so once it is installed your agent can discover and use them. Dynatrace also publishes a dedicated MCP server for its platform intelligence; enable it per your agent's MCP configuration if you prefer an MCP transport over the CLI. The toolkit never requires Davis AI — plain DQL is enough to run the whole loop. The intelligence layer only makes query authoring faster.

Python 3.12 — only if you run the engine from source (binaries and the Docker image bundle their runtime). See engine.md. A load tool — k6 (native fit), or JMeter / Locust / Gatling, depending on which renderer you use. The synthesis skills fall back to node --check for static validation when the tool binary is absent. Node.js — to run the renderer skills' test suites (node --test). A coding agent — Claude Code, opencode, Cursor, or any agentskills.io-compatible agent. See skills-install.md.

Produces a single Gatling Simulation class in Scala plus JSON feeders. Arrival profiles map to constantUsersPerSec / rampUsersPerSec (open) or constantConcurrentUsers / rampConcurrentUsers (closed, with max concurrency from Little's Law). Journey mix becomes a randomSwitch; correlation uses .check(... saveAs) into session attributes. Payload pools become JSON feeders materialized as a Zipf multiset so .random reproduces the hit ratio. synthetic=true is set as an HTTP protocol header alongside W3C trace-context propagation. Arrival model open and closed, native Feeders / payloads JSON feeders as a Zipf multiset reproducing the hit ratio synthetic=true httpProtocol.header("baggage","synthetic=true") + trace-context Declared approximations per-step exponential/empirical think-times fall back to a mean pause; HTML-DOM extraction falls back to regex See skills/gatling-synthesis and How it works for where this sits in the loop.

The engine is the deterministic core of SCOPE: a standalone, dependency-light program. It is backend- and tool-agnostic: it reads a neutral telemetry extract (JSON) and emits a G0-gated workload-model.json plus a human-readable scenario-proposal.md. It never talks to Dynatrace or to a load tool — a backend adapter (e.g. the dtctl/DQL pack) produces the extract; a renderer skill turns the approved model into a runnable test. Where it lives: skills/workload-model/ (SKILL.md + scripts/ + tests/). Language: Python 3.12. Runtime dependency: jsonschema only (bundled into the released binaries and the Docker image). Interface: reads an extract JSON, writes workload-model.json + scenario-proposal.md to an output directory, supports --mode agentic|commerce. The released workload-engine binary and the ghcr.io/henrikrexed/ai-performance-testing Docker image package this skill so you can run SCOPE without a Python toolchain. From source you run the skill directly (see §1 From source). Binaries and the image are produced by the release workflow — there is nothing to build by hand.
Pick one. Released artifacts are published per version tag on the Releases page by the release workflow.

# amd64 (use workload-engine-linux-arm64 on ARM hosts) VERSION=v0.1.0 curl -fsSL -o workload-engine \ "https://github.com/henrikrexed/AI-Performance-Testing/releases/download/${VERSION}/workload-engine-linux-amd64" chmod +x workload-engine sudo mv workload-engine /usr/local/bin/ workload-engine --help

VERSION=v0.1.0 # Only an Apple-Silicon (arm64) binary ships. Intel Macs: run it under Rosetta 2, or use Docker. curl -fsSL -o workload-engine \ "https://github.com/henrikrexed/AI-Performance-Testing/releases/download/${VERSION}/workload-engine-darwin-arm64" chmod +x workload-engine # first run on a downloaded binary: clear the quarantine flag xattr -d com.apple.quarantine workload-engine 2>/dev/null || true sudo mv workload-engine /usr/local/bin/ workload-engine --help

$Version = "v0.1.0" Invoke-WebRequest ` -Uri "https://github.com/henrikrexed/AI-Performance-Testing/releases/download/$Version/workload-engine-windows-amd64.exe" ` -OutFile "workload-engine.exe" .\workload-engine.exe --help

The image is published multi-arch (amd64 + arm64) to GHCR: docker pull ghcr.io/henrikrexed/ai-performance-testing:v0.1.0 # or :latest # mount a working directory; extract.json goes in, results come out under ./out docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/work \ ghcr.io/henrikrexed/ai-performance-testing:latest \ --extract /work/extract.json --out /work/out

Run the engine as a one-shot Job, mounting the extract via a ConfigMap and collecting output from a volume (or an emptyDir + a sidecar/kubectl cp). Minimal manifest: apiVersion: batch/v1 kind: Job metadata: name: workload-model spec: backoffLimit: 0 template: spec: restartPolicy: Never containers: - name: engine image: ghcr.io/henrikrexed/ai-performance-testing:v0.1.0 args: ["--extract", "/work/extract.json", "--out", "/work/out"] volumeMounts: - { name: extract, mountPath: /work/extract.json, subPath: extract.json } - { name: out, mountPath: /work/out } volumes: - name: extract configMap: name: workload-extract # kubectl create configmap workload-extract --from-file=extract.json - name: out emptyDir: {} kubectl create configmap workload-extract --from-file=extract.json kubectl apply -f job.yaml kubectl wait --for=condition=complete job/workload-model --timeout=120s kubectl logs job/workload-model # prints the G0 report + PASS/FAIL The image runs as a non-root user and needs no network or cluster permissions — it is pure compute over the extract you give it.

git clone https://github.com/henrikrexed/AI-Performance-Testing.git cd AI-Performance-Testing/skills/workload-model pip install "jsonschema>=4,<5" # bundled synthetic example: extract -> G0-validated model + proposal python3 scripts/build_example.py cat out/example-frontend/scenario-proposal.md python3 -m pytest -q # the engine's own test suite

The engine owns SCOPE. It is one stop in the methodology's SCOPE → VALIDATE → SYNTHESIZE → EXECUTE → ANALYZE loop (full detail in methodology.md). The engine's job is to produce a model that a human can approve.
documents.s: 2. Use — the engine in the loop

documents.t: Point your backend adapter at a clean telemetry window (service, timeframe, environment) and capture the facts the engine needs — journeys/span-trees, archetype split, per-minute arrival counts, baselines. The reference adapter is the dtctl/DQL pack — see requirements.md §2 and the skills/workload-model SKILL.md; any backend that emits the same JSON shape works. skills/workload-model/fixtures/example_extract.json is a complete synthetic extract showing the exact schema.
documents.s: Step 1 — produce a neutral extract (adapter, outside the engine)

documents.t: # released binary workload-engine --extract extract.json --out ./out --mode agentic # from source, equivalently: # (cd skills/workload-model && python3 scripts/build_example.py) --mode agentic splits Agentic vs. Conversational turns on the execute_tool terminal signal; --mode commerce splits Buyer vs. Browser on the order-terminal service. Same engine, different terminal signal. Outputs land in the output dir: workload-model.json — the schema-valid (§4 v1.1) model: journeys + weights, open/closed arrival profile with Little's-Law check, payload pools, and hard caps. scenario-proposal.md — the human-readable proposal (what was analyzed, journeys, arrival profile, payload strategy, where it will run, risks, decision requested). The engine self-checks with the G0 gate and prints the result. It exits 0 only if G0 passes, non-zero otherwise — so it is safe to gate a pipeline on the exit code.

No test runs before a human approves the model. A person reads scenario-proposal.md and approves, adjusts, or rejects. Approval is bound to the model revision — there is no agent self-approval, and any later edit invalidates a prior approval. This gate is the point of the whole methodology; keep it.
documents.s: Step 3 — VALIDATE (the mandatory human gate, V1)

documents.t: Once approved, hand workload-model.json to a renderer skill (skills/k6-synthesis, jmeter-synthesis, locust-synthesis, gatling-synthesis) → a runnable test where every request carries baggage: synthetic=true. Then skills/loadtest-run executes it under allowlist + hard caps + automatic abort, and skills/baseline-diff compares the run shape against the observed baseline (V3), deciding accept / iterate (parameter-only, ≤3×) / escalate.
The engine is also the single entry point for onboarding and for driving the whole loop as a conversational flow — no manual symlinking, no remembering the renderer entrypoints.

# two commands total: fetch + install skills, then drive curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/henrikrexed/AI-Performance-Testing/main/install.sh | sh install.sh clones the repo (or downloads the tarball when git is absent) and runs engine/cli.py init, which copies every skill into your agent's skills directory and verifies it. The default destination is ~/.claude/skills (the Claude Code user-wide path from skills-install.md); override with --dest (e.g. .agents/skills for the cross-client location) or AIPT_DEST=…. # from a checkout, equivalently: python3 engine/cli.py init # -> ~/.claude/skills, then verifies python3 engine/cli.py init --dest .agents/skills

python3 engine/cli.py guided \ --extract examples/crewai-deepseek-agent/extract.json \ --out ./out --mode agentic # add --renderers k6,jmeter,locust,gatling The flow is the methodology loop, gated: Propose + confirm — builds the model, prints a readable summary + the full scenario-proposal.md, and stops at the V1 human gate. Approval is bound to the model revision (canonical hash of spec); the renderers fail closed without it. Confirm interactively, or --yes in CI/scripts. No confirm ⇒ nothing downstream runs. Choose output — --renderers (default k6; one or several). Only k6-synthesis is bundled today; jmeter/locust/gatling follow the same renderer-kit interface and the flow hands them the approved model once their synthesis skills are installed. Generate — renders the runnable project via the renderer skill's entrypoint when its toolchain is present, otherwise prints the exact command. Try it? — opt-in only (--try): a few seconds of a real k6 smoke, else the command to run it yourself. Production runs stay behind loadtest-run's allowlist + hard caps + auto-abort. A machine-readable guided-state.json records each step (and the honesty invariants: revision-bound confirm, synthetic=true baggage, opt-in run) so a coding agent can narrate the flow.

Symptom Cause / fix G0 FAIL + non-zero exit One or more G0 criteria failed — read the printed checks[]; usually a coverage gap or an unlinked step in the extract. jsonschema not importable in the G0 report Only happens from-source without the dep — pip install jsonschema. Binaries and the image bundle it. macOS "cannot be opened / unidentified developer" xattr -d com.apple.quarantine workload-engine (binaries are unsigned). Docker: --out empty on the host Mount a writable host dir to /work and point --out inside it (--out /work/out). See methodology.md for the full gate and safety specifications.
KnightLoad is a five-stage loop. Each stage has one owner and one gate, so you always know what just happened and what has to be true before the next step runs.

Stage Owner Input → Output Gate SCOPE you / your agent clean telemetry window → workload-model.json + scenario-proposal.md G0 extraction self-check VALIDATE a human, always reads the proposal → approval bound to the model revision V1 human approval SYNTHESIZE you / your agent approved model → runnable test + synthetic payload pools V2a static checks EXECUTE you / your agent small confirmation run, then a capped, abort-guarded full run V2b smoke gate ANALYZE machine + human cap shape-diff of test vs baseline → accept / iterate / escalate V3 tolerance eval

SCOPE. Query a clean telemetry window and extract the facts a realistic test needs — journeys, archetype split, arrival profile, think-times, and payload strategy — into a workload-model.json. VALIDATE. A human reads the proposal and approves, adjusts, or rejects it — this is the gate the whole method exists for. SYNTHESIZE. Turn the approved model into a runnable, committed test with synthetic payload pools — deterministic codegen, never an LLM "generate" prompt. EXECUTE. Run a small confirmation test first, then a capped, abort-guarded full run against a non-production target. ANALYZE. Shape-diff the test run against the observed baseline and decide: accept, iterate, or escalate.

Nothing runs until a person approves it. After SCOPE, KnightLoad stops and shows you a scenario-proposal.md: what it analyzed, the journeys and their weights, the arrival profile, the payload strategy, where the test will run, and the risks. You approve, adjust, or reject. That approval is tied to the exact revision of the model you read. If the model changes afterward, the approval no longer counts and synthesis refuses to proceed. There is no agent self-approval and no "approve by telemetry." This one gate is the point of the whole methodology.

The engine (workload-model). The deterministic core: it runs the extraction, clusters journeys, shapes the arrival profile, and self-checks the result with Gate G0 (coverage, per-step evidence source, Little's-Law consistency, a schema-valid model). It exits non-zero if G0 fails, so you can gate a pipeline on it. Runs as a released binary, a Docker image, or from source. The renderers (renderer-kit + the four exporters). One interface, one model as the sole contract. Each renderer turns the approved model into a runnable test for a specific tool and declares its approximations up front. See Exporters. The run harness (loadtest-run). Enforces the non-production allowlist, hard caps, automatic abort, and the V2b smoke gate before any full run. The analyzer (baseline-diff). Shape-diffs the run against the baseline across the tolerance dimensions and returns the V3 verdict. The skills. Agent-skill packages (skills/*/SKILL.md) you install into a coding agent so it can drive the loop in plain language — doing the legwork, never the deciding. See Installing the skills.

KnightLoad prefers two sources fused: spans give trace topology and structure; access logs (Istio/Envoy sidecar + ingress) give the authoritative, instrumentation-independent HTTP record and a request-id correlation backbone. For session boundaries, action order, and think-times it reconstructs sessions from whatever signal is present, in preference order: RUM ordered user actions — richest signal; needs the RUM read scopes. OTel session.id on spans — Grail-native, app-agnostic, no extra token. Span-order fallback — where no session signal exists, and it records the gap. The model records which source drove each endpoint, so provenance is auditable rather than blurred. And the caveats are carried openly: extraction is only as good as the telemetry window you choose, and full session fidelity depends on a session signal being present end-to-end — where it's sparse, think-times and ordering degrade to span-order assumptions. That's a known limit, not a hidden one.
documents.s: Where the numbers come from (honest about fidelity)

documents.t: Every generated request carries OTel baggage synthetic=true, promoted to a span/resource attribute so it is queryable. The ANALYZE step uses that filter to separate generated traffic from the real baseline inside the same environment — your test traffic and your real traffic never blur.
documents.s: Traffic you can always tell apart

documents.t: The skills/* directories follow the agentskills.io convention: each is a directory with a SKILL.md (the instructions the agent loads) plus deterministic scripts and tests. An agent "installs" a skill by having its directory on the agent's skills search path. Skills in this repo: Skill Stage What it does workload-model SCOPE telemetry extract → G0-gated workload-model.json + proposal k6-synthesis · jmeter-synthesis · locust-synthesis · gatling-synthesis SYNTHESIZE approved model → runnable test (one renderer-kit interface) loadtest-run EXECUTE scoped run: allowlist, hard caps, auto-abort, run report baseline-diff ANALYZE DQL shape-diff vs. baseline, accept / iterate / escalate rum-sessions · session-stitch SCOPE (RUM) RUM session shape & ordered-action reconstruction Which renderers ship today: k6-synthesis is bundled and wired end-to-end (the guided flow generates a runnable k6 project headlessly). jmeter/locust/gatling follow the same one-interface renderer-kit contract; install their synthesis skills the same way and the guided flow hands them the approved model. Pick your renderer in the guided flow's step 2.

No manual symlinking. One command installs the skills into your coding agent; the second is the first prompt that starts the guided loop. # 1 — fetch the repo and install the skills into ~/.claude/skills (verifies them) curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/henrikrexed/AI-Performance-Testing/main/install.sh | sh install.sh clones the repo (or downloads a tarball when git is absent) and runs engine/cli.py init, which copies every bundled skill into your agent's skills directory and verifies each one loads. The default destination is ~/.claude/skills (the Claude Code user-wide path); override with --dest or AIPT_DEST. From an existing checkout the no-curl equivalent is: git clone https://github.com/henrikrexed/AI-Performance-Testing.git cd AI-Performance-Testing python3 engine/cli.py init # -> ~/.claude/skills, then verifies python3 engine/cli.py init --dest .agents/skills # cross-client location instead init prints the exact next command. The second command of the quickstart is that prompt — start the guided 4-step flow (see engine.md §3): # 2 — drive the gated loop on the bundled synthetic example (no backend needed) python3 engine/cli.py guided \ --extract examples/crewai-deepseek-agent/extract.json \ --out ./out --mode agentic …or, with an agent that now has the skills, just ask in plain language: "Use the workload-model skill to build a model from the example extract." That is the whole onboarding. The manual per-agent copy steps below remain for CI, locked- down boxes, or agents whose skills directory differs from the defaults.

Each coding agent discovers skills from a conventional directory. Install = copy (or symlink) the skill directory there. Paths below follow the same standard the Dynatrace CLI uses (dtctl skills install --list). git clone https://github.com/henrikrexed/AI-Performance-Testing.git cd AI-Performance-Testing

# project-local (this project only) mkdir -p .claude/skills cp -r skills/* .claude/skills/ # or user-wide (all projects) mkdir -p ~/.claude/skills cp -r skills/* ~/.claude/skills/ Claude Code auto-discovers every ~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md (or the project-local .claude/skills/) and loads a skill when the task matches its description.
# project-local mkdir -p .opencode/skills cp -r skills/* .opencode/skills/ # or user-wide cp -r skills/* "$HOME/.config/opencode/skills/" # --global location
# project-local (Cursor discovers project skills, not user-global ones) mkdir -p .cursor/skills cp -r skills/* .cursor/skills/

The portable location — discovered by any compatible agent (Claude Code, opencode, Cursor, Copilot, Kiro, Junie, …) without per-agent copying: # project-local mkdir -p .agents/skills cp -r skills/* .agents/skills/ # or user-wide mkdir -p ~/.agents/skills cp -r skills/* ~/.agents/skills/

Ask your agent to run the bundled worked example — if the skill is installed, it will pick it up by name: "Use the workload-model skill to build a model from skills/workload-model/fixtures/example_extract.json." Or run a skill's tests directly to confirm the files are intact: ( cd skills/workload-model && python3 -m pytest -q ) # 68 passed ( cd skills/k6-synthesis && node --test test/*.test.mjs ) # 51 passed Installing these skills is separate from installing the dtctl agent skill (which ships with the CLI via dtctl skills install). See requirements.md §3.
